Before September 4, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-then Leader of the Opposition-would visit the Eastern Townships and the Bois-Francs region, harping on his favourite theme: job creation.
He promised to spur the asbestos sector, spoke of more active development in forestry, guaranteed that textile and footwear industries would be protected, and committed himself to creating more jobs as a result of better promotion of agri-food business through more intensive research. Practically in the same breath, the Conservative Party emphasized the need to boost and support those sectors whose main objective is external trade-Domtar and asbestos, among others. This region was also slated to become a strategic centre since the cartographic institute was to become reality.
Here is the tally after six months in office. Jobs: hundreds have been lost, thousands more are about to disappear. Asbestos: nothing whatsoever has been done. Footwear: quotas have been slashed. Cartography: the project is under review. Agriculture: pork producers are still waiting for their cheques. Research: Victoriaville's $14 million research project has been cancelled. Domtar: not a single Quebec Minister knows what is going on.
Yet, we are amazed at the haste with which $40 million were handed out to Kruger in the Maritime Provinces, not to mention the $73 million to a western bank, and over $600 million in defence expenditures to please the Americans.

Mr. Speaker, I am certain that Members of Parliament, and indeed all Canadians, will join in the appeal brought to us yesterday by the Jewish Students' Network in Canada on behalf of Soviet Jewry. With the emergence of the new Soviet leader, Mr. Gorbachev, we can be hopeful that there will now be an opportunity for a relaxation in the Soviet Union's policy which would permit the emigration of Jews who wish to go to Israel. A realistic goal would be the reinstatement of the Soviet policies of the late 1970s which permitted large numbers of Soviet Jews to leave for Israel.
We also welcome the statement made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) indicating that he intends to take up the case of the Soviet Jews with Soviet authorities when he visits the U.S.S.R. next week. During his visit, I would urge him to endeavour to arrange to meet with the Jewish "Refusenik" groups so that he and we can be briefed on their present difficult situation.

Mr. Speaker, the new agreement on oil and gas pricing in Canada initialled yesterday by the Minister of Energy (Miss Carney) and her provincial counterparts in western Canada is further evidence of the Government's positive record of success.
Hear, hear!

This agreement, like the Atlantic Accord, is proof that consultation and co-operation are the way to achieve positive results. For over four years, agreements of this nature eluded the previous administration.
Since September Canada's economy has witnessed growing signs of strength. The unemployment rate has fallen. Investment confidence is strengthening. Consumer spending and manufacturing orders are rising, and interest rates have dropped.
There are tough economic decisions that lie ahead of us, but those decisions will be made after listening to the people of Canada and getting their advice and opinions. The recent

March 27, 1985
economic conference was an opportunity for Canadians to be heard and for politicians to listen.
On September 4 last, the people of Canada placed their confidence in this Government. We have achieved much in seven months. We will achieve more in the next four years.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to urge the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to hand in his resignation to the new Progressive Conservative Government. Requested by the Government to cut $75 million, the President failed to show any understanding for the plight of isolated areas where the service is inadequate and the unemployment rate has reached astronomical proportions as a result of Liberal waste and the absence of any economic policy for 20 years.
Unfortunately and predictably, the cutbacks were apparently not carefully considered, and I have the impression that the nonchalant way our region was dealt with is only the tip of the iceberg. I am therefore convinced that those who helped to "fatten" the system and expand this corporation cannot be expected to have the ability to manage negative growth and take a more reasonable approach.
Since the way the cutbacks are made is more important than the actual amounts involved, I think it would be perfectly legitimate to ask the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to give the new Progressive Conservative Government a chance to appoint a president more attuned to this country's new political and economic principles.
The President of the CBC should therefore have the courage to respond to the demands of a new Canadian reality, as of September 4, because in addition to the $75 million cutbacks, Canada needs an entirely new management style in public affairs, and the new Government should not be expected to take every manager by the hand to put Government spending in 400 Crown corporations and 40 departments on a more rational footing.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is very fond of consultation as we all have noticed. Few major initiatives have been taken by a government paralyzed by indecision and uncertainty. However, there is a consensus in Canada the Government has not yet discovered, a consensus supported by all Canadians, and I am referring to the view that more women should be appointed to decision-making positions on the boards of Crown corporations, in government agencies and on commissions. This is a genuine consensus that is supported by all the polls.
Even if the Government keeps giving us the assurance that appointing women to management positions is one of its priorities, that is obviously not what is happening. Last week, at Air Canada, only one of thirteen appointees was a woman. That is 7 per cent, Mr. Speaker. On a committee of experts in botany, two out of eight appointees were women and this was two out of five at the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.
Incredible!
If the Government is so keen on governing by consensus, it should appoint women to decision-making positions, and it would certainly be a good thing for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in 1981 Parks Canada initiated the Four Mountain Parks Planning Program to develop long-range management plans for Banff, Jasper, Kootenay, and Yoho National Parks. This program included extensive public consultation during which the vast majority of participants rejected wholesale tourist-oriented development within these parks in favour of little or no development, in keeping with Parks Canada's own mandate which puts first priority on ecological and historical integrity. The consensus in this regard was overwhelming, yet Parks Canada ignored popular will and recently proposed a prodevelopment management plan for the four mountain parks block. Is the new parks policy of the Conservative Government to ignore public opinion, to turn our national parks into Disneylands, and to sacrifice our environmental heritage to the market-place?
The year 1985 is the 100th anniversary of Parks Canada. All Canadians are justifiably proud of our national parks, and this should a be a year of celebration. Instead, ever since the election of the Tories, a dark, disturbing cloud of cut-backs, insensitivity, and uncertainty, has descended on our national parks system. I call on the Government to respect the mandate of Parks Canada, the wishes of the majority of Canadians, and our environmental heritage, by rejecting Parks Canada's prodevelopment scenario for Banff, Jasper, Kootenay, and Yoho National Parks.
March 27, 1985

Mr. Speaker, for over 100 years Canada has stood as a rock of freedom in an often troubled and tormented world. This country was built by hardworking, dedicated individuals who came to Canada because they could be free here, free to prosper, and free to speak out and participate in a democratic society that treated them as equals. For many, the greatest freedom of all was the freedom to worship in their own way.
Last week in my riding I met with a group of people whose friends and relatives, who live in another country, are being persecuted because of their religious beliefs. They spoke of the torture, killings, and beatings which have been perpetrated by the Government on these religious followers. All these people want is the freedom to worship God in their own way.
To us in Canada religious freedom is a basic and fundamental right. Yet, for millions of people around the world it is not. Let us always be mindful and thankful of the freedoms and rights for which this country has proudly stood. In addition, let us, as Canadians, remain committed to maintaining our freedoms and continuing to set an example for other countries of the world.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: GENESIS OF RECORDING TO ASSIST AFRICAN FAMINE VICTIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the power of music is used to soothe, to uplift, and to seduce. Now, Canadian musical artists have combined their talents to use the power of music to persuade Canadians to help feed the starving people of Africa.
We have all heard the record Tears Are Not Enough, the Canadian music community's response to an international call for help. I am proud to inform the House that the genesis of this unique venture occurred in my riding of Capilano, British Columbia. There, world acclaimed producer David Foster wrote the words, while Bryan Adams and Jack Vallance created the music. Others such as Bruce Allen and Terry David Mulligan formed the Northern Lights for Africa Society which will donate the proceeds from the sales of the record, the video, and the CBC documentary on the making of this record, to the African Famine Relief.
Fifty-five Canadian artists gathered together in a studio on a cold February afternoon and spent 15 hours to record the song, without recompense, and forgoing other engagements. Anne Murray, Cory Hart, Robert Charlebois, and Liona Boyd are just some whose generosity is only exceeded by their artistry.
Yes, we have a new hit in the Canadian recording industry, but it will be Canadians across the country who support this venture and transform music into dollars for famine relief. In the words of the song:
We can learn to share
And show how much we care
We can make the difference
Don't you know that tears are not enough?

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Commissioner of Official Languages tabled his annual report. At that time he stated:
The Canadian Government, indeed Canadians generally, need to wake up to the fact that progressive polarization threatens the probable extinction of most French-speaking minorities outside Quebec and, by ricochet, drastic reductions of the English freedoms within that province.
That is an alarming statement for both English and Frenchspeaking minorities. However, I would like to advise the House that the ricochet effect has already started.
For some time the Anglophone minority in Quebec have been subject to repeated attacks on their language rights. Since 1981, 90,000 Anglophones have left that province. The situation has been equally critical for our French-speaking brothers in other provinces.
As well, the Commissioner made the following pleas. He urged the new Tory Government to use its financial and regulatory clout to extend bilingualism in the private sector. He urged the Government to help Canadians who go to the courts seeking delivery of minority language rights under the Charter of Rights. Finally, he urged the Government not to undercut language reform through spending cuts in the Budget which is to be brought down in May.
We support these measures and we urge the Government to respond positively to these recommendations as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians watched with appreciation yesterday as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) and her provincial counterparts announced in principle a new energy accord with the producing western provinces. This agreement is the result of skilful leadership by the Minister. It also fulfils another of my Party's election promises, that is, a new approach to energy development in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Why did the Prime Minister allow his Minister to hang in the wind yesterday, because he was not able to respond directly? Was it because there is a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs? speechtext:

Given the different time zones and time frames, I think any fair minded person would agree that obviously net everything is instantaneous. Having said that, I think there is no doubt but
that the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs has set out the position of this Government on that and other issues, with great courage, thoroughness, and dignity. I salute him for that because I know that that calm and reasoned approach finds favour with the Canadian people, and I hope with my right hon. friend.

subtopic: YOUTH-USE OF FUNDS FOR JOB CREATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: YOUTH-USE OF FUNDS FOR JOB CREATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that the Prime Minister did not answer the question. I have a supplementary.
If Canada were to participate in U.S. Star Wars research, this would oblige the Government to spend several billion dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money on a U.S. arms program. It would be naive to think otherwise. Would it not be better to spend those billions on creating jobs for our young Canadians?

subtopic: YOUTH-USE OF FUNDS FOR JOB CREATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Leader of the Opposition will agree that the Government is going to do what he probably would have done himself in similar circumstances. When we receive a request from our allies, we discuss it in Cabinet and make a decision as soon as our schedule permits. We have just received this invitation. I am now going to submit it to my Cabinet colleagues, and we shall announce our decision to the House in the near future.
For instance, we recently received a request from the Prime Minister of Israel and from Egypt, asking us to consider the possibility of replacing the Australian contingent on a peace mission in the Middle East. That is a proposal, an invitation we have just received. We are going to submit it to Cabinet and we shall announce our decision in due time.

subtopic: YOUTH-USE OF FUNDS FOR JOB CREATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course the Secretary of State knew about Israel's invitation because it was made to him directly. I might say that this Party would support the Government's participation in replacing the Australians in that particular enterprise.

The
Prime Minister said, or is reported to have said, that if star wars will create jobs then we should consider taking part. That is how he was reported. Does the Prime Minister think that there is some burning desire among Canadians, particularly young Canadians, to make a living off the escalation of the nuclear arms race?

Mr. Speaker, what I said was that if a proposal were brought forward consistent with the requirements of the ABM Treaty which

could create, say, 10,000 jobs in Winnipeg-Fort Garry, we would take a look at it.
Unless my right hon. friend is saying that job creation and the dignity of human beings in Canada are unimportant, and I do not believe that, and unless he is suggesting that this Party is a Party of warmongers, after we fought off the Liberals on the question of nuclear arms-remember Mr. Diefenbaker fought you to a standstill and prevented nuclear arms from coming into this country. That is the position of this Party.
The last time nuclear arms were allowed on Canadian soil, it was by the Liberal Party of Canada, and Canadians will never forget it. That is the difference between you and I.
Mr. Speaker, it is very easy for the Prime Minister to rewrite history, but we are dealing with the problems of today.
Oh, oh!
I was there at that time. I was not a backroom boy; I got elected in those days.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister is seriously considering the Americans' request for us to participate in star wars, will he live up to the reputation of Canadians, that we have always been on the side of peace, and not get into an adventure which will lead to escalation of the arms race around the world?

We are very conscious of the tradition, in which this Party has played an honourable role, of searching for a durable peace in the world. I think my hon. friend would agree that it was not the most glorious moment in the distinguished history of the Liberal Party when it reversed itself and accepted nuclear arms on Canadian soil. I know you would be as ashamed of that today as you were then.
So was Pierre Trudeau.

In fact a very distinguished Canadian, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau, then a very distinguished journalist, said that the Liberals were the defrocked princes of peace for what you did on the nuclear arms issue.
This Party will always be here to protect the integrity of Canada and make sure that our approach to the quest for a durable peace is always serious and at the top of our priorities.

Mr. Speaker, I was around in those days and 1 remember the Minister of Veterans Affairs having to resign because the Diefenbaker Government broke its word. The same thing happened with the resignation of Douglas Hark-ness, who had to resign because Mr. Diefenbaker was breaking his word.

Mr. Speaker, I am asking the Prime Minister if he is about to break the word of this Parliament, given a year ago when he was Leader of the Opposition, when all in this House agreed that Canada would never participate in any way, shape or form in star wars?
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend should go back-

Yes, he is rewriting history, not of years ago but of months ago.
Three weeks ago he said they were against it.

I take seriously the observations of my hon. friend. I think he would take seriously the fact that, because it is not a partisan matter, we have no lessons to learn from anyone in regard to our commitment to the strength of our allies and the sincerity of our desire to be of assistance in the procurement of a durable and honourable peace. There is nothing more important to Canadians, irrespective of their political views, and nothing brings Canadians together with more certainty than the assurance that this Government, any national Government, is deeply and irretrievably committed to a genuine search for a peaceful solution and de-escalation of nuclear tensions in the world. Nothing is more important, and we are committed to that to the fullest.
Why are you reversing yourself?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last year, following the patronage appointments by Messrs. Trudeau and Turner of over 200 Liberal individuals, the Prime Minister indicated that he had joined the majority of Canadians who were sick and tired of this kind of partisan appointment to serious jobs. At that time he said specifically that if he were elected he would make a basic change in the whole approach. Since then there have been Conservative appointees to Air Canada, Via Rail, the Senate, and Citizenship Courts, to name just a few. Instead of 200 appointees, we have now had over 1,000 Conservative appointees.
More! More!

They are yelling "more". More pigs at the trough, that is what they are yelling on the other side. Where is the change? Why is Conservative patronage any better than Liberal patronage?

March 27, 1985
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, before my hon. friend dissolves in exasperation, I would like to tell him that I have spent a very long weekend looking for Conservative appointments made by the NDP Government of Manitoba.
Hear, hear!

Try as 1 might, Mr. Speaker, and I have a fine eye in this matter, I could not find a single one. In contrast, this Party has appointed distinguished people like Stephen Lewis, and Mrs. Gold to the chairmanship of the Committee on the Status of Women. Long after these people opposite should have done so, we recognized the distinguished service of Tommy Douglas and appointed him to the Privy Council of Canada. Many other distinguished NDP members have been appointed, and there will be more, because we believe that the Public Service and these appointments should reflect the best of Canada.
Having said that, I have been talking to my friend, a very distinguished parliamentarian, the Member for St. John's East, who, with his task force on parliamentary reform, will hopefully be bringing forward some mechanism that will allow us all to improve on what was a very sad and sorry Liberal record.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the facts stand for themselves. To understate it, 95 per cent of the appointees whom the Government has named have been Conservatives. The Prime Minister knows it. The only reason they got the appointments was because they were Conservative, and the whole country knows that as well.

Mr. Speaker, last October the Government froze the wages of all the working people in VIA Rail so that they could make their contributions to the viability of the government of that entity. Having done that, how could the Government announce, just two days ago, that the new chairman of VIA Rail, a former Conservative candidate, would have his salary increased to $135,000? Why is there one sense of justice for ordinary workers and another for Tory patronage?

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member were to be fair, I think he would recognize that it has been my privilege, as Prime Minister, to make more non partisan appointments in six months than any of my predecessors whom anyone in this House can remember.
Hear, hear!

Lawrence Hanigan is widely regarded as an outstanding leader in mass transportation in Canada. If I
recollect accurately, the Montreal Gazette pointed out with considerable pride the accomplishments of Mr. Hanigan in this field. He is a very distinguished Canadian and Quebecer who, it is true, once stood for the Progressive Conservative Party. Given his remarkable record of accomplishments over a long period of time, I do not think that that should disqualify him from serving as chairman in an area of public endeavour where he has received such high marks over the years. 1 think you should be standing up and congratulating us for this fine public service appointment.

The Prime Minister should go to all the workers in VIA Rail and explain to them why they should have their wages frozen while this man gets an increase up to $135,000 a year. Let him explain that to the working people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary question concerns a sacred trust that the Prime Minister entered into during the television debates. He said: "A series of appointments should be looked at attentively by House of Commons committees." "I propose to you tonight," he said to the people of Canada, "that this notion be extended so that all political appointments, for example to the CTC, be approved by a House committee." A sacred trust. How could the Prime Minister make that commitment on the one hand and then, after he obtained office, appoint Marcel Lambert, a former Conservative MP, to the CTC? In addition to his response, will he tell us that there will be no more such appointments coming from the Government until he sets up a committee to vet all such appointments?

You signed all right-with invisible ink.

Mr. Speaker, if I may, I recognize in the gallery the presence of the distinguished Mayor of Westmount. But that is no reason for the Prime Minister to insist on forgetting that my riding is Saint-Henri-Westmount. I am sure the mayor would agree with that.

We feel that the result will be extremely good for western Canada, eastern Canada, and all Canadians, in terms of bringing this country together and creating the economic growth to create the jobs that are needed.

As far as the profitability of the oil companies is concerned, they have demonstrated a willingness to reinvest these profits in the Canadian economy to find oil and gas production, as well as to create the jobs that Hon. Members

are asking us to encourage. Surely you cannot have it both ways. Either the oil companies will do what is right for the country and create jobs, or they will take their money and go elsewhere. We want them to leave their money here, create the jobs, and find the oil and gas production.

subtopic: INVESTMENT BY FOREIGN OWNED OIL COMPANIES
INVESTMENT BY FOREIGN OWNED OIL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the majority of the oil industry is still foreign owned and those big multinationals will benefit by going to the world price because they will get a windfall when their old oil moves to the world oil price.
Is the Minister prepared to introduce real legislation that will require these foreign oil companies to reinvest the windfalls they will get, in Canada? Will he also indicate to the House whether he is prepared to protect the consumer in the long run when the price of oil is liable to skyrocket again if there is an OPEC oil crisis, now that we are dependent on the OPEC price? Will he protect the consumer in the long run from the effects of drastic increases in this free market for oil?

subtopic: INVESTMENT BY FOREIGN OWNED OIL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Hon. Member asked two questions. First, are we confident that the oil companies will reinvest their cash flows into the Canadian economy and create the jobs? Yes, we believe they will. My colleague, the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources, and I have had extensive discussions and we are confident that they will do that and that they will create the jobs that we need here in Canada.
The second part of the question, I believe, was whether there would be some protection for the consumer in the event that, under price decontrol, there was a spike in the oil and gas price. That is something we propose to do.

Mr. Speaker, the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages was tabled in the House yesterday. The least that can be said is that it is an alarming report for francophones, for a bilingual Canada, and for those who believe in linguistic equity.
Considering that the Federal Government must set the example and be the driving force in linguistic matters, can the Prime Minister tell the House whether he intends to introduce a Bill in the not too distant future with a view to reinforcing the powers of the Commissioner of Official Languages to enable him to promote, encourage and even require linguistic equity, or, to put it another way, to meet the wishes of Canadians to have a public service sector that closely reflects the example they are giving?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague is raising a very important issue. In the November Throne Speech, we indicated that as a Government we feel that bilingualism has to be a vital aspect of our national existence, a sentiment that is widely shared, 1 believe. Like my colleague, I am concerned about the undoubtedly justified remarks of the commissioner and, this morning, I asked the Deputy Prime Minister to make early arrangements to convene all Deputy Ministers in the Public Service so that we might undertake an operational analysis to enable us to define the parameters required for such a Bill.

subtopic: FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
In his report the Commissioner of Official Languages mentions the progress we have made in Canada in the language of education and the language of communication, and he raises the important question of the language of work in the Public Service of Canada.
Is the Government prepared to explain to the Committee on Official Languages Policy and Programs its policy concerning the important question of the language of work in the Public Service of Canada?

subtopic: FRENCH AS LANGUAGE OF WORK IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not look into that aspect of the question, but I think it is a very reasonable suggestion. If people cannot work in French, it is a myth, and everything must be done to maintain the integrity of that instrument, that cultural and linguistic wealth, either by coercion, or by making sure that it will be sought after as an instrument of work. He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the Government to move second reading of this Bill which I believe is an important and significant piece of legislation. The Bill is brought before the House as a result of the enactment of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which occurred in 1982. Also in 1982, certain provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms-which is now the ultimate law of the land in Canada-particularly those relating to equality matters, were not to come into full force and effect until April 17, 1985, in order to give Governments across the country an opportunity to prepare for the massive changes which will result in Canada and to the system of laws as a result of the enactment of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The federal Government, provincial Governments and territorial Governments, once the Charter had been proclaimed, undertook to review their legislation, regulations and administrative practices to ensure that they were consistent with the Charter as far as it could be determined. As a result of the review which has taken place in the Government of Canada, a broad range of federal initiatives were undertaken to bring about conformity with the Charter. This Government assumed office last September and it has moved as quickly as possible to ensure that Canadian laws reflect the values which are enshrined in the Charter.

There has been the criticism that we are not moving quickly enough. As a matter of fact, the critic for the Official Opposition wrote to people across Canada suggesting that they should not appear before the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which the House has appointed and requested to do the job of looking at Equality Issues in Federal Law: A Discussion Paper. That paper has been referred to the subcommittee in order that it can take representations from the public across Canada, to involve them in consultation, dialogue and what should be the answers to the policy issues which are raised in the paper. The critic of the Official Opposition actually wrote to groups across Canada suggesting that they not appear before the committee or give their views to the committee because the committee was unnecessary. As he is a member of that committee, I suppose he is hoping that he will have an easy time of it if no one appears before it.
I want to point out that the project of reviewing federal statutes to discover if they comply with the Charter commenced on April 1, 1982. That is when the human rights law section was established in the Department of Justice. For over two years our predecessors were in charge of the operation of reviewing federal statutes to discover whether they complied with the Charter in so far as that could be determined. Of course, the courts will ultimately determine whether they do or do not comply.
I can assure the House that there were no concrete proposals left behind by the predecessor Government with respect to that question. As well, there were no answers left behind by that Government to the questions which are raised in the discussion paper. I would say to the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), who is the official critic for the Official Opposition, that if he has any answers he should give them in committee. If he can give quick answers to these intricate quesions, then the committee can report very quickly if it decides that his answers are correct and can be acted upon. As a matter of fact, he said that the Liberal Government was ready to implement laws. The peculiar thing is that the Department of Justice was instructed by the Liberal Government to examine
Statute Law Amendment Act
issues and not to reach conclusions or suggest solutions. The Department was asked to examine the statutes of the Government of Canada to discover if they were in conflict, in any respect, with the Charter and not to provide conclusions as to how the policy questions which were involved were to be answered. I hope, if the Hon. Member for York Centre does have the answers, that he will present them to the committee and it can then report to us.
What is the Bill about? The Bill is to ensure that federal statutes which are obviously in conflict with the Charter will be amended so that the conflict will no longer exist. This Bill contains amendments to over 50 federal statutes. It is the result of the examination of more than 1,100 Canadian statutes.
Action has already been taken in certain areas. For example, the Criminal Code amendments, which are now under consideration by the Department of Justice, have already dealt with the issue of the abolishment of writs of assistance. Other initiatives are under way to ensure consistency with the Charter. As Members will know, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) introduced amendments to the Indian Act which will end discrimination, against Indian women. Those amendments are now before a standing committee of the House of Commons.
In addition, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) will be bringing forward amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. When that is done, certain provisions of that Act, which we feel are in breach of the Charter, will be amended.
The Chief Electoral Officer and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) are currently looking at the Canada Elections Act with respect to Charter concerns as well as other changes. That Act is now being considered by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
Officials of the Departments of Finance and National Revenue are reviewing certain seizure provisions in the Income Tax Act and related statutes. When that legislation is brought before the House for amendment in connection with the next Budget, the legislation will also be amended in connection with any provisions of the legislation which we believe offend the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Another statute which is being dealt with separately with reference to Charter concerns is the Emergency Powers Act. Obviously, that is a difficult area and a comprehensive review is required.
From time to time the Criminal Code of Canada will be amended and Charter issues will be part of that continuing review. By 1987 or 1988 we are aiming to have the project of reforming the Law Reform Commission study and the reformation of the Criminal Code of Canada complete. We intend to deal with Charter concerns in the ongoing Criminal Code review.

Of course, the last initiative is the one which I mentioned earlier, the document which is entitled Equality Issues in Federal Law: A Discussion Paper. That has been referred to the special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
The Charter guarantees equality, but it does not indicate how equality will be achieved. We believe that the people of Canada have a right to be heard on the complex policy issues which are outlined in this discussion paper and on other such issues which may be brought forward by anyone who appears before the committee. We think the public should be involved before changes are proposed in areas such as mandatory retirement and with respect to what should be done with pensions and annuities as a result of the fact that women generally live a longer life than men. The public should be involved in any decisions taken with respect to the question of gender discrimination-if that is the right description-in the armed services. The armed services have certain rules which do not permit persons to continue in the armed services who may be lesbian or homosexual. These are some of the difficult policy issues on which the committee will be asked to express an opinion.
In adopting this procedure, we are being the opposite of elitist. We are giving minorities a chance to be heard. I have heard some criticism, Mr. Speaker, from those who are active in women's groups and other groups that this is unnecessary. Well, it may be unnecessary for those particular persons. They are obviously interested in these kinds of public issues. They have studied them. They are at the forefront of the movements for women's rights, rights for the handicapped or visible minorities or whatever it may be. What we want to do through this committee, Mr. Speaker, is to involve the ordinary men and women of Canada in these issues. That is the purpose of having the committee. These persons have a right to be heard and we are giving them a chance to be heard.
There are some people who have said-I don't know how this twisted reasoning came about, how they could go from one supposition to the other-that we are permitting the majority to tyrannize the minorities. That would be a criticism, of course, of the whole parliamentary process and history certainly demonstrates that the reverse is true. It is Parliament, the House of Commons, which has responded to the needs of minorities throughout Canadian history. It is this House of Commons which responded to the needs of the minorities when the Charter and the revised Canadian Constitution was being considered in 1981-1982. The Charter itself was adopted through the parliamentary process. To suggest that we should not have a parliamentary committee consider equality issues which are controversial and raised by the Charter is certainly a peculiar bit of reasoning indeed.
I want to make it plain, Mr. Speaker, that we are not asking the committee for legal opinions. That is not what the committee was appointed for. The courts will give us the definitive legal opinions on matters which may arise under the Charter which are not clear or are in dispute. It is the Charter itself which raises the question, "What is reasonable in a free and democratic society?" We know that there are many situations of discrimination or discretion and choice throughout our legislation and our policy. The question is whether it is proper discrimination, discretion and choice. With respect to many of these issues the final question is going to be, "What is reasonable in a free and democratic society?"
In a free and democratic society, is a mandatory retirement age contrary or not to the Charter? On the face of it, it is contrary to the Charter because if there is a mandatory retirement age, it is a discrimination against those who are being forced to retire. The question then becomes, "Is that a reasonable rule in a free and democratic society"? That is not a legal question, Mr. Speaker. It is a question which anyone in the country can have an opinion on and your opinion, Mr. Speaker, is just as good as mine. Normally, I would not admit that, but today I do admit that anyone's opinion on issues like these are just as valuable as another person's. One doesn't have to be a Ph.D., a great lawyer at one of the bars of this country or particularly skilled in any direction to have a view as to whether mandatory retirement is a fair and reasonable rule in a free and democratic society.
Those are the kinds of questions which the committee, chaired by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), will have to seek answers to and make its recommendations. The other members of the committee, just for the record, are: the official critic for the Opposition, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan); the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), the official justice critic for the New Democratic Party; the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes); the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Clinch); the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins); and the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Tremblay). It is a seven-member committee and those members of the committee are going to have their hands full, Mr. Speaker, because these are pretty complex questions.
The paper sets out a number of programs and policies which are reflected in Canadian laws which may be flawed in light of the equality guarantees in the charter. We are asking the committee to get information and views from Canadians as to whether they think these laws should be changed and, if so, how they should be changed. It is the role of the committee in Parliament to make policy choices among the competing options, keeping in mind the charter guarantees. It is the views of individual Canadians which are essential if we are to make the best possible choices. This is for us to do, not the courts. We are not asking the parliamentary committee to do the job which the courts will be asked to do.
Before I forget, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record the names of some of the people in the Department of Justice who did the hard and gruelling work of examining
March 27, 1985

1100 statutes to see where conflicts might be, making recommendations, preparing this equality paper and preparing the legislation. They are Clare Beckton, who is on loan to us from Dalhousie University; John Scratch; Carole Johnson; Stan Cohen; Stephen Sharzer; Barbara Hough and Michele Joub-ert; Lewis Seale looked after communications; Assistant Deputy Minister John Tait; and Martin Low, who is general counsel for human rights law in the Department.
The names of the drafters of this particular piece of legislation should be on the record as well and they are Guy Laurin and Francois Lafontaine. These are the people we have to thank for the hard work which has gone into this paper, Mr. Speaker, and it was very hard work. They had to deal with every other Department and agency in the Government of Canada in ways which are very complex.
I mentioned the criticism that somehow we were tyrannizing the minority by having this sub-committee. That is such a silly argument, I think it deals with itself. The committee is going to have to deal with the question of what is reasonable in a free and democratic society with reference to these particular issues. It is social policy which we are asking the committee to deal with. We are not suppressing minorities. The committee is giving the minorities a greater opportunity to put forward their views on these particular issues. In this Bill we are acting where it is wise to act. Through the discussion paper we are consulting where it is wise and necessary to consult.
With respect to the Department's review of the statutes, I am not claiming that this is some stroke of genius of mine. We have only been in the Government for the last six months. It was the decision of our Liberal predecessors, with which I agree, that the statutes should be reviewed based on the assumption that it was preferable to change questionable legislation rather than leave it to individual litigants to assert their rights in court. That involves costs, delay and hardships. So where it is clear that legislation is questionable, we are now changing it so it does not have to be challenged in court, and there are a lot of areas where it is not clear.
Of course, we want to avoid disruption of important government programs because of adverse court decisions. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in trying to decide whether or not some particular provision of the legislation is au fait with the Charter, there are very few decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada to go by. So it is a difficult proposition because we do not have many precedents in Canada to go by, although you can look at the U.S. precedents for some assistance.
The provisions proposed for amendment here are clearly contrary to Section 15 and do not involve complex social and economic concerns. The complex concerns will be dealt with by the subcommittee. It is also worth keeping in mind that the Charter does not dictate solutions in this area. It sets certain minimum standards and our committee is going to have to consider taking those standards into account in deciding what substantive policy should be reflected in our laws.
Statute Law Amendment Act
What are some of the provisions dealt with in this legislation? We deal with powers of entry in federal statutes. Do not think this is an unimportant piece of legislation because it is not. It deals with many important areas. Powers of entry in federal statutes such as the National Defence Act and the Canadian Human Rights Act are dealt with. There are also provisions to ensure that all Bills the Government presents to the House, and all regulations, are examined to ensure that they are consistent with the Canadian Bill of Rights and the Charter.
This is only one part of the over-all approach I described to try and ensure Charter conformity. There are a number of federal statutes which presently authorize entry to premises without a warrant, and other places, to ensure compliance with the regulations or evidence of contravention of statutes. The issue here is whether the guarantee in the Charter against unreasonable search and seizure in Section 8 is violated by these provisions.
In this Bill we are treating differently those powers of entry which authorize an inspection as against those which authorize a search. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in a routine matter an inspector will come to see if you are complying with some statutory regulation. It might have to do with agricultural or dairy products, or they might be coming in to examine the books. In those kinds of cases we believe a warrant should not be required unless the inspection is taking place in a private dwelling. If it does take place in a private dwelling, there should be a warrant. People who work in closely regulated activity expect to be inspected regularly, but there has always been a distinction between dwelling places and other premises.
So there are amendments in this Bill to statutes such as the Fish Inspection Act, the Canada Grain Act and the Textile Labelling Act which provide for a warrant when you are making a non-consensual entry for an inspection. That means that the person whose premises you are inspecting has not consented. A search will occur if an entry is made to seek evidence of a contravention of a statute. We are amending those federal statutes which contain search powers to provide that you must have a warrant when you wish to enter a building to seek evidence of a contravention of a statute.
We also spell out when a warrant will not be required. If a delay in obtaining a warrant will result in danger to human life and safety, or in the loss or destruction of evidence, then a warrant would not be required. The courts will, of course, have the opportunity to review whether or not those kinds of circumstances existed. There are changes to the Fisheries Act, the Environmental Contaminants Act and the Migratory Birds Convention Act in connection with inspection powers in those Acts. So the purpose of these amendments is to provide for reasonable searches, but in the meantime to provide that legitimate inspection functions in agriculture, fisheries and the environment will not be hindered.
There are important amendments to the National Defence Act. For example, the major changes provide for a greater degree of equivalence between the code of service discipline and the criminal law. I would just give one example. The

March 27, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
amendments provide that any accused may have the benefit of any defence available under the Criminal Code or any other federal law if the person is being tried on a charge under the code of service discipline. That is a major change. The legislation will end double jeopardy. It will permit an accused to plead that he has previously been acquitted or convicted or punished by a service tribunal, a civil court in Canada or by a court of competent criminal jurisdiction in another country. That was not the case before. I will not mention some of the other changes because of the quick passage of time, and I do not want to be too long in introducing the Bill.
There are amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act which reflect the Canadian tradition of procedural fairness. These changes have to do with a situation where the Commission finds a complaint to be substantiated and then appoints a tribunal to look into that particular complaint. Since the Commission presently makes a decision whether the complaint is substantiated and also appoints the tribunal, there is a possible perception that the Commission is making a finding of guilt before requesting the appointment of a tribunal. Now, under the new procedures and these amendments, the Human Rights Commission will screen complaints and determine whether a tribunal should be appointed. But we provide for an independent office, the president of the tribunal, who is independent of the rest of the Commission and he will now appoint a tribunal from persons listed and it will be done independently and appear to be done independently. It will give a better perception than the present provisions provide. By the way, the Human Rights Commission has been supportive of that amendment.
I am glad to see the official critic of the NDP is here even though his Official Opposition counterpart is not.
The Bill also deals with a number of areas where, quite clearly, equality provisions of the Charter were being violated; changing references to members of one sex, where there is no justification, to exclude members of the opposite sex; changing words such as "wife" to "spouse", "widow" to "surviving spouse", in various acts such as the Canada Shipping Act and so on. There is another group of amendments which deal with age. In the Canada Corporations Act the age 21 is replaced by age 18 as their criterion for pilotage and so on.
The Minister of Justice already has an obligation under the law to examine Bills and regulations to ensure they are consistent with the Bill of Rights. I am referring to the Bill of Rights enacted under the late great John Diefenbaker when his Government was in power. These amendments provide a similar obligation on the Minister of Justice to examine regulations and Government Bills to ensure they are consistent with the Charter. That is new. They also provide for the co-ordination of the examination of regulations under the Statutory Instruments Act, the Department of Justice Act and the Bill of Rights.
Then there are a whole set of other miscellaneous amendments. For example, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has the power to suspend or cancel leases or licences. There is a change being made there. The right of the Minister to order
forfeiture is abolished. There are amendments to the Immigration Act to provide that when there is an inquiry of an adjudicator, and we heard of such as inquiry today, it will be held in public unless it is established that the person concerned or some Government interest would be adversely affected. The bar against action for false imprisonment in the Canada Shipping Act is removed and there are other amendments of that type.
Let me again emphasize that this Bill is not put forward as our sole initiative in ensuring consistency of federal laws with the Charter. There will be many other pieces of Government legislation in this session dealing with Charter issues. Of course, as decisions are made on the issues that come before the courts, we will have to act. One example which comes to mind is with respect to the Customs Tariff item which, about 10 or 12 days ago, was found by the federal Court of Appeal to be contrary to the Charter provisions with respect to the concept of immoral and indecent when people bring goods into the country. The House will have to amend the customs legislation in that respect.
As a result of court decisions, in the future the House will have to make changes in legislation from time to time. We also recognize that there may be aspects of federal legislation that we missed in this review. It is a continuing process to ensure conformity with the Charter. New problems will be identified from time to time. I have an open mind on the need for further changes and in connection with the nature of changes that we or other Members of the House may propose.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to move second reading of this Bill. I am a bit disappointed at the reaction of the Official Opposition to the steps we have taken, particularly since they were exactly the steps that they were going to take. They have not offered any suggestions for any different steps in the last six months. However, their ranks are rife with hypocrisy and hypocrisy is often their standard on issues such as this.
I was shocked by the actions taken by the Member for York Centre. As I mentioned earlier, he had the audacity to write to groups across the country suggesting that they not take an interest in this matter and not appear before a House of Commons subcommittee. I have never heard of any Members of the House writing to groups across the country trying to persuade them not to appear before a committee that the House had decided to set up. I am happy to realize that no one has paid any attention to his advice in that respect. I am delighted that other members of his Party, such as the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), are demonstrating more interest in the matter than is the official critic. 1 know the Hon. Member for Mount Royal will be following the issues closely.
If the official critic for the Opposition can give answers to the issues raised in the discussion paper or can persuade the subcommittee to accept some good, sound, sensible policy advice, then the committee can make interim reports from
March 27, 1985

time to time and we will be pleased to prepare the necessary amendments. The subcommittee has been asked to report at the end of August. It may find that it needs more time. If so it will have only to report to the Government and House asking for an extension of time. It can make an interim report and go on to deal with the matter in more depth.
Evidence of the seriousness with which we take this matter is shown by the calibre of the Members that we on this side have appointed to the committee. The Chairman himself is a distinguished lawyer with a great interest in this particular subject. We have appointed the Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), who is one of our women Members. I suppose I am allowed to mention that without being held to be discriminatory. We also have the Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes), who is another of the Canadian women who were elected to the House in the last election of September, 1984. We on this side of the House are very glad to have a very healthy representation of women. We want more, of course, and will have more as the years go by. Two of the five Members whom we have on this subcommittee are women members of the PC caucus. We notice that the Opposition have appointed all male Members to represent them on the committee, although the Hon. Member for Mount Royal will be appearing in substitution.

It is obvious that Hon. Members opposite are very sensitive about this Bill. It is quite obvious why they are sensitive.
It is also interesting to note that the Minister of Justice spent a great deal of time defending Bill C-27. He was correct in doing so because, in my respectful submission, Bill C-27 is quite simply a cop-out. It is a cowardly act on behalf of the Government because it is afraid to make tough decisions that are necessary with respect to equality in this country. Rather than providing the necessary leadership, the Government has introduced a Bill that basically does very little. In effect, all the Bill does-and is there any wonder why the Minister had to go on the defensive because he had nothing good to talk about with respect to this Bill-is change the language in the various pieces of legislation. I believe the Minister indicated there are about 50 pieces. It changes "husband" and "wife" to "spouse". It changes the words "son" and "daughter" to "child". What it does not do is address the very important issues facing this country concerning equality rights.
This Government had a choice. This Government could have taken definitive action as a result of the extensive audit initiated by the previous Government and as a result of the work done by the Justice Department to indicate the inequities and parts of the various pieces of legislation that do not conform to the Charter. The Government could have made a decision on issues such as mandatory retirement, sexual orientation, combat roles in the Canadian Armed Forces and whether those roles should be open to women. But this Government refused on the pretext that it had to consult and on the pretext that it wanted more information from the Canadian people.
In my submission the Government was afraid to lead, it was afraid to make decisions. Instead, it opted for a consultation process which, in my view, is a cop out. It appears the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are afraid to make those very important decisions. The Government is afraid to alienate any individual in society. Therefore it has decided to put off the issue of equality rights for many months, if not years. April 17, 1985 will be upon us in a few short weeks. The supreme law in this country, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, will be law. No federal majority, not even the Conservative majority we have today, can over-rule the supreme law of this country.
Of course, there is the over-ride provision in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but I would hope this Government will not exercise that over-ride position, as the Government of Quebec has done consistently since 1982.
What does Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provide? There are 46 words in Section 15, a mere 46 words, but the importance of those words is indeed tremendous. Section 15(1) reads as follows:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in

March 27, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, or mental or physical disability.
That will become law on April 17. At the Constitutional Conference of 1982, as a result of compromises and considerable conflict resulting from the compromises, it was decided to put off the implementation or proclamation of Section 15 for three years. This was in order to give the federal Government and the 10 provincial Governments the opportunity to audit their respective legislation and there was the understanding that that legislation would be brought into conformity with Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
What has happened, Mr. Speaker? You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that there were certain Conservative provincial Governments that fought tooth and nail for the entrenchment of rights and freedoms in the Constitution. Those same Governments are continuing to procrastinate and delay and are doing everything in their power to obstruct the implementation of this section.
Specifically, what have the provinces done since 1982? We know the province from which I come, Ontario, which has a Conservative Government for a few short weeks longer-

What has British Columbia, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island done? Those Governments have done absolutely nothing. This suggests to me and to the people of Canada that those Governments are not sincerely interested in or concerned about equality rights in Canada.
What has the federal Government done? As I indicated previously, the previous federal Government initiated an audit of the approximately 1,100 federal statutes in order to determine the extent to which those statutes would contravene the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It was the intention of the previous Government to make the tough decisions and to implement the laws that would change the old laws to bring federal legislation in conformity with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Unfortunately for the issue of equality in this country, the Conservative Government came to power on September 4 with an overwhelming majority, with a mandate from the Canadian people to make decisions, with a mandate from the Canadian people to provide the leadership that they were promised. What do we have, Mr. Speaker? We have a total lack of leadership with respect to the issue of equality rights in this country. This Government has opted basically to do nothing. This Government has opted to force the minority groups, the women, the visible minorities, the young, the disadvantaged and the disabled to fight their battles again when all these groups in 1982 came forward and fought. They fought hard. They got their Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They thought the battle was fought and won. They thought the wounds of discrimination that have existed for so long were beginning to heal. They thought that discrimination was coming to a rapid and quick end. What has happened? This Government is intentionally reopening those wounds of discrimination. This insensitive Conservative Government is forcing those groups, the women, the visible minorities, the disadvantaged, the young, the old and the Indian groups to come forward and fight their battles again. That is totally unfair.
I agree wholeheartedly with my colleague from York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) who said to those groups that this Government is not interested in the issue of equality. If you want to ensure and protect your right, Mr. Speaker, you must go to court and let the courts determine what equality means. Let the courts define what Section 15 means.
Those people have been provided with no alternative. This Government is continuing to procrastinate on these very fundamental and very important issues facing the country. The sad part is that the Government is forcing these people to litigate, which is not a desirable consequence. We, the 282 elected Members of Parliament, should be making the decisions, not the courts of law. We represent all the good people of Canada and we should be the advocates of civil rights, human rights and equality. We should protect the minority groups. It is the 282 individuals in this House of Commons who should be making the decision, not having the courts defining Section 15 in a purely legalistic manner.
These people have no option but to go to court. There is no option but to have a court of law make a decision to interpret equality in their particular case based on a particular set of circumstances. What makes matters worse is that the Government refuses to establish a fund. It will not put money aside to assist these people, who for the most part are not affluent, so that they can litigate.

Mr. Speaker, I would have expected the Hon. Member to know better. This troupe will be travelling across the country. What can result from this exercise in futility? As Shelagh Day, a community activist, said, you do not define minority rights by majoritarian views and values. That is not the way to do things.
What will happen as a result of this committee? The majority of Canadians might say that they do not believe in mandatory retirement. There may be a minority which says that mandatory retirement is necessary. They might talk about combat roles for women in the Armed Forces. The majority of Canadians might believe that women should not be enlisted in the Armed Forces. Precious little comfort that is to the women who want equality in the Armed Forces. Precious comfort that is to the women who want the right to get involved in combat roles.
What is this committee going to do? Will the committee say that because the majority of Canadians say no, therefore equality does not mean that women are entitled to get involved in combat roles in the Armed Forces; or is the Government going to say that, notwithstanding what the majority says, it believes women should have full equality when it comes to the Armed Forces? Given its actions, I believe this Government will opt for the former rather than the latter option. It is afraid to offend people. It believes that minority rights in this country are defined by majoritarian views and values.
The Charter is important because it involves the protection of individual rights. Although Canada has one of the best records anywhere in terms of safeguarding the rights of its citizens, we must never become complacent. In many places around the world it is a sad fact that rights are too often proclaimed and too seldom protected. Countries that have constitutions with glowing affirmations of human rights are often the same countries where violations of basic rights are an every day occurrence. It has been said many times that the price of freedom is eternal vigilance. The protection of rights is indeed one of the most solemn duties we face in a free and democratic society.
As I indicated previously, on April 17, 1982 the Constitution Act was proclaimed in this country. A tremendous step forward was taken at the time in terms of protecting the rights of future generations. The Act provided for the patriation of the British North America Act from the United Kingdom but, more importantly, it included a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In my respectful opinion that Charter is second to none in the world.
The patriation of our Constitution was largely a symbolic gesture since Canada has long been regarded as a sovereign and independent nation. However, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was intended to have a more direct impact on our daily lives. Why was the Charter necessary? The answer is

March 27, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
quite simply that Canadians wanted their rights enshrined in the Constitution. It was recognized at the time that full equality was not a reality in this country. In a great many cases only lip service was paid to the concept.
We wanted a Charter because we as a nation believe in freedom and equality and we believe profoundly in justice. The Charter is merely and affirmation of that fact. It is a statement of principles entrenched in our most basic law. It is intended to protect individual rights and freedoms each and every day as part of a living, breathing constitutional document.
As Hon. Members know, when the Constitution Act was proclaimed in 1982, the implementation of this part of it was delayed for three years. That was one of the political compromises that was necessary in order to entrench the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in our Constitution. April 17 of this year could be a more historic and momentous day if the Government opposite would take the definitive action necessary to ensure that full equality becomes a reality in this country.
The implementation of Section 15 attests to our full maturity as a free and democratic nation. The words of Section 15 form the core of one of the most significant parts of the resolution, a part that former Prime Minister Trudeau called the people's package. Canadians have cause to be proud of this Charter because it is indeed one of the best in the world. It is the legacy of Mr. Trudeau, a testament to his political courage and determination.
Much more could have and should have been done by this Government to enshrine full equality in the laws of Canada. There was a great deal of hope and anticipation on April 17, 1982 when the constitutional resolution was proclaimed by the Queen. We all recall that very momentous and historic day.
I sense none of that same mood as we approach the date for the proclamation of equality rights. At the end of three years, Canadians were expecting the federal Government to present a Bill containing the necessary amendments to the laws that fail to comply with the provisions of the Charter. What Canadians expected and what the Government is offering through Bill C-27 are two different things. Many laws, both provincial and federal, still to this day contravene the equality rights provisions contained in Section 15.
In some respects, the foot dragging on equality rights on the part of the federal and provincial Tories should not come as a surprise. As I indicated previously, five of the Tory provincial Governments opposed the constitutional resolution and fought against it tooth and nail. Sterling Lyon of Manitoba was particularly adamant that there should be no constitutional guarantees of any rights whatsoever. There were many supporters of his point of view among Conservative Members of this House, many of whom are still here today. 1 take comfort in the knowledge that Hansard faithfully recorded their remarks. Indeed, it must be difficult for these Members who opposed the Constitution to witness their own Tory Government carrying on where Mr. Trudeau left off with respect to enshrining equality rights provisions, albeit the Government is
carrying on meagrely and modestly, as shown by this proposed legislation.
We all know that the dinosaurs within the Tory caucus were brought into line once a deal had been struck with nine of the ten provinces. One of the aspects of that deal between the federal Government and the provincial Governments was the three-year delay. Those Governments are continuing to procrastinate and delay. Where there should have been substantive measures put forward, we have a Bill that falls desperately short of the mark. Bill C-27 falls far short of what is necessary in order to guarantee full equality in the Constitution. The Bill constitutes an exercise in language reform rather than a true application of the spirit of the Charter.
The policy questions that were raised in the document entitled Equality Issues in Federal Law are the policy questions that should have been decided by the Government. This legislation does not address age discrimination as it relates to mandatory retirement or sexual discrimination as it relates to pension contributions for women in the Public Service. It does not address the issue of whether requirements relating to the length of employment or maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act should remain greater than requirements for regular benefits. It does not deal with the issue of whether combat roles in the Canadian Armed Forces should be open to women. It does not address the question of whether mental or physical disability ought to be a bar to immigration in some circumstances. It does not come to grips with whether native Canadians should remain effectively excluded from participation in the Canada Pension Plan because participation is tied to income as defined in the Income Tax Act and earnings on a reserve are non-taxable. Bill C-27 does not deal with whether persons should continue to be excluded from the Canadian Armed Forces on the basis of their sexual orientation.
There are many, many unresolved issues in many areas of discrimination based on race, ethnic origin and physical disability that remain completely untouched by Bill C-27. In many respects, April 17, 1985 will be a sad day for justice and equality in this country.
The Government could have corrected the inequities and injustices that continue to exist in our free and democratic society. It could have dealt bigotry and racism a body blow. It could have told the provinces to bring their legislation into line and it could have led by example. Instead, it has left all of the tough decisions out of Bill C-27. It has put them off into yet another subcommittee and discussion paper for further review and further public hearings.
I was not present in the House three years ago as were many Members opposite. They know about the many hours of debate that took place with respect to the Constitution and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They know and will remember well representatives of dozens and dozens of different organizations coming to Ottawa to make their views known. Now the Tories want to repeat a significant portion of that process. The purpose of this exercise is questionable but we all know what the results will be. The results will be more
March 27, 1985

procrastination and more delay. Delay is a key word because justice delayed is justice denied, and justice is being denied to all those groups that are suffering from discrimination in this country.
The Tories are paralysed with fear about doing the wrong thing. So they do nothing so as not to offend anyone. They are afraid to lose a seat or two. They are afraid to go to bat for minority groups. They are prepared to take on popular causes, but they are afraid to go to bat for the people who are suffering. We all know that consultation is important. It is a vital element in the legislative process. Governments should not take precipitous or hasty action for the sake of appearing decisive. That was the fatal flaw of the nine-month Tory Government. Neither should Governments let consultation be an end in itself. A balance must be struck, otherwise the consultative process becomes like molasses in the decisionmaking machinery of Government. It gums up the works and nothing gets done.
In conclusion, I wish to reiterate the serious concerns which my Party has with respect to this legislation. We will, of course, support the legislation because it will tidy up some of the language in the legislation which now exists. However, we will continue to press for full equality. We want to ensure that equality becomes a reality in the very near future. We disagree profoundly with the procedure which is being proposed by the Conservative Government. If it were truly interested and sincere about equality, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) would be in the House to listen, and the Government would take the definitive action which is so necessary.
I look forward to further discussions with respect to this legislation in committee. I am sure that other members of the Official Opposition will have more to say on Bill C-27.

Mr. Speaker, I had the honour four years ago, as a relatively new and young Member of Parliament, to sit on an historic committee. That committee was the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada. That committee was charged with the responsibility of reviewing a proposed constitutional resolution and hearing not only witnesses with respect to the proposed Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but also the provinces and other concerned groups about the constitutional process.
I recall vividly the fact that witness after witness came before the committee-whether they were representatives of native people, minorities, women's groups, or the disabled-to urge the Government to strengthen the resolution which had been tabled in the House. That resolution was strengthened. The equality rights section of the Constitution was improved significantly.
The constitutional package came into effect on April 17, 1982. It was felt that Governments needed three years, until April 17 of this year, to bring their legislation into compliance with the provisions of Section 15, the section which deals with equality rights. We waited three years, but I would suggest
Statute Law Amendment Act
that when this Government finally moved on January 31 it was a black day for human rights in Canada. What it constituted was a bitter betrayal of the hopes of women and minority groups in Canada who had hoped that the Government would take its responsibilities seriously, not simply to review legislation, but where the review showed that the legislation was in conflict with the fundamental principles of equality, that the Government would bring forward changes.
I would like deal briefly with the arguments which were made by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata). I appreciate that he is a new Member and that he was not present for some of the debates which took place subsequent to the passage of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As Members, we have been witness to the most extraordinary rewriting of history which this Chamber has probably ever seen. That Member stood and attacked the Government for refusing to move on issues of concern to minorities. He attacked the Government for listening to the majority and refusing to heed the concerns of minorities, including the disabled and the minority which is discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.
I would like to remind Members of what really happened and of the history of the Liberal Party after the passage of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The history of his Party, when it was in Government, was a history of explicitly and deliberately denying the claims to full equality for the groups which the Hon. Member for York South-Weston now stands up self-righteously to defend. What is the record? I would like to give the House a couple of examples.
A special parliamentary committee was struck to look into discrimination against the disabled. That committee tabled in the House a report which was entitled Obstacles. That report very eloquently documented the history of abuse and inequality. I would like to salute the members of that committee. In my view they did an outstanding job of bringing to the attention of Parliament and the Canadian people discrimination, both economic and social, against the physically and mentally disabled people of Canada.
That report was tabled in 1981. I would remind Members of the House that the Liberal Party was in Government from 1981 until 1984. I would ask the Hon. Member for York South-Weston-who has attacked the Conservatives for doing nothing to assist the disabled in the country-where was he and his Party when the disabled people said that it was time for action? For him to suggest that they were prepared to take action to remedy the historic injustices against the disabled, when they did nothing for three years after the tabling of the report, surely to goodness Canadian people must recognize that something is wrong.
The Hon. Member for York South-Weston said that this Government was copping out on human rights and fundamental justice. He accused the Government of listening to the views of the majority. Both of those criticisms, Mr. Speaker, may be well founded but, I recall vividly, as a member of the Justice Committee-and the Hon. Member suggested we should look at the records of the justice committee-hearing
